莊子說苑卷三

<margin>This is the conduct of a person of ultimate virtue, who does not seek fame or achievement. Why then, master, are you pleased by being heard?</margin>
blamed for it. The person of ultimate virtue is not heard, master; why are you pleased by it? Confucius said, "Excellent!" and declined the invitation. He 
<margin>Does not prize luxury</margin>
ceased his associations, left his disciples, and fled to the great marshes. He wore clothes made of coarse fur and ate acorns and chestnuts. 
<margin>Does not prize delicacies</margin>
<margin>Does not cultivate a heart of discrimination that disrupts the flocks of birds and beasts.</margin>
Entering among beasts, he did not disturb the herd; entering among birds, he did not disrupt their flight. Since the birds and beasts did not dislike him, how much more so 
<margin>Even creatures of a different kind do not dislike him.</margin>
<margin>Surname/Name: The Recluse</margin>
would people? Confucius asked Zisang Hu, "I was twice banished from Lu, had the tree cut down over me in Song, had my traces erased in Wei, was reduced to poverty in Shang and Zhou, and was surrounded in the lands between Chen and Cai. Having suffered these several calamities, my relatives and associates have become more distant, and my followers and friends have scattered. What is the reason for this?" Zisang Hu

<summary>This page recounts Confucius's dialogue with the recluse Zisang Hu, emphasizing the virtue of the hermit who lives in harmony with nature and avoids the political entanglements that brought Confucius so much suffering.</summary>
